response.text:
Controlled evidence supports testing samplers, but I found no direct validation that a frozen, training-only lexical/popularity difficulty audit predicts held-out ranking gains. [Prakash et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) compare uniform, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling with hyperparameter optimization and 20 repeats across three datasets: aggregate performance can conceal opposing head/tail effects. [HNS theory and experiments](https://doi.org/10.1145/3543507.3583223) connect BPR hard-negative sampling to partial-AUC optimization and recommend controllable hardness; this does not establish that greater training difficulty always improves ranking. [gSASRec](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/301348/3/301348.pdf) reports popularity-sampling benefits under popularity-sampled evaluation that did not transfer to full-catalog metrics, illustrating evaluator dependence.

Recommended controlled NextItNet ablations: uniform baseline; popularity-matched random negatives; lexical negatives matched on training-frequency bins; uniform plus a modest fraction of lexical negatives; model-scored semi-hard negatives from a fixed-size pool. These are proposed controls, not a literature-established optimal recipe. Hold architecture, loss, negative count, updates, seed and evaluator fixed; train one model/category per variant. Build lexical features and popularity counts exclusively from permitted metadata and training interactions; exclude known training positives. Freeze identical audit histories/candidate pools and report margins, violation rates and popularity strata, but select using the pinned macro validation HR@10. Lexical similarity or high model scores cannot identify actual false negatives: [UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116) motivates that risk, although its teacher-based method falls outside this experiment. Interpret improving training margins without validation gains as evidence against the sampler hypothesis, not proof of better preferences.
